content: Yersinia pestis is a rod-shaped, facultative anaerobic bacterium that exhibits bipolar staining, giving it a characteristic safety pin appearance under the microscope. It is responsible for causing infections in mammals, including humans. The bacterium's life cycle is maintained through interactions between rodents and their fleas. Yersinia pestis belongs to the genus Yersinia, which is part of the Gram-negative, bipolar-staining coccobacilli group. Like other members of the Enterobacteriaceae family, it has a fermentative metabolism. This bacterium produces an antiphagocytic slime layer, which aids in its virulence. While it is motile when isolated, it becomes non-motile once inside a mammalian host. Taxonomically, Yersinia pestis is classified as follows: Bacteria; Proteobacteria; Gammaproteobacteria; Enterobacteriales; Yersinia; Yersinia pestis. Biologically, Yersinia pestis is a non-motile, non-spore-forming, Gram-negative bacillus that does not ferment lactose. It has an ovoid shape and displays a safety pin appearance due to its bipolar staining. On cell cultures, it grows as grayish translucent colonies on sheep blood agar and can also grow on MacConkey agar and nutrient-rich broths. However, it is highly sensitive to environmental factors such as high temperatures, sunlight, and disinfectants, surviving only a few hours on physical surfaces. Yersinia pestis is believed to have evolved from Yersinia pseudotuberculosis approximately 1,500 to 2,000 years ago. Based on its nitrate and glycerol metabolism, Yersinia pestis can be classified into three biovars: Antiqua (nitrate reduction positive, glycerol reduction positive), Medievalis (nitrate reduction negative, glycerol use positive), and Orientalis (nitrate reduction positive, glycerol use negative). The complete genomic sequences of two Yersinia pestis subspecies are available: strain KIM (biovar Medievalis) and strain CO92 (biovar Orientalis). As of 2006, the genome of a strain from biovar Antiqua has also been sequenced. These genomes show evidence of mutations leading to loss of function. The chromosome of strain KIM is 4,600,755 base pairs long, while that of strain CO92 is 4,653,728 base pairs long. Like other Enterobacteriaceae, Yersinia pestis harbors the plasmid pCD1. Additionally, it carries two unique plasmids, pPCP1 (also known as pPla or pPst) and pMT1 (also known as pFra), which are not found in other Yersinia species. The pFra plasmid encodes a phospholipase D enzyme critical for flea-borne transmission, while the pPla plasmid encodes a protease (Pla) that activates plasminogen in human hosts, playing a key role in the virulence of pneumonic plague. Together with a pathogenicity island called HPI, these plasmids encode several virulence factors essential for bacterial adhesion, injection of proteins into host cells, invasion of host cells via a Type III secretion system, and acquisition of iron from red blood cells through siderophores. A comprehensive proteomic analysis of Yersinia pestis strain KIM was conducted in 2006, focusing on its adaptation to growth conditions mimicking those within host cells. Yersinia pestis exhibits a tropism for lymphoid tissue. The natural reservoir of plague is primarily rodents, with the infection persisting in wild rodent colonies through transmission by their flea ectoparasites. Images from the Public Health Image Library (PHIL) depict various aspects of Yersinia pestis, including Gram-negative bacteria grown on sheep blood agar, ulcerated skin lesions at plague inoculation sites, blood smears showing the presence of the bacterium, and histopathological changes in lymph node and lung tissue samples from fatal human plague cases. Additional images show chest X-rays of pneumonic plague patients, acral gangrene caused by the bacterium, and Yersinia pestis on the proventricular spines of Xenopsylla cheopis fleas.
